evidence_spans: In the present work, we used in situ scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), corroborated with atomistic simulations, to study in real‐time and at the atomic scale the structural and compositional evolution of AuCoCuNiPt NPs from 298 to 973 K.
These in situ insights into the thermodynamic properties of AuCoCuNiPt HENA reveal their poor structural stability at high temperature due to atomic diffusion that cannot be considered as sluggish.

evidence_spans: In the present study, the same HENA was directly synthetized on the SiN membrane of a heating MEMS chip commercialized by Protochips for in situ TEM investigations.
A substrate temperature of 873 K, a laser frequency of 5 Hz, and a total nominal thickness of 4 nm measured prior to metal deposition were measured with a quartz crystal microbalance.
A few tens of nm‐large TiO 2 NPs were deposited on the SiN membrane by drop casting prior to the synthesis of HENA in order to facilitate area recognition during in situ TEM experiments.
TEM observations were performed at 473, 673, 773, 873, and 973 K and a heating rate of 1 K s −1 was used to reach these temperature steps.
As HENA continuously evolves at high temperatures, the analysis time at each temperature was limited to 45 min.

We had to go back to 298 K after each temperature step to perform EDS analyses to avoid the adverse effect on the X‐ray detection efficiency of IR radiation emitted from the heating device at high temperatures.

evidence_spans: Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K.

Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature.

This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.

evidence_spans: At low temperatures (500 K), a solid solution is clearly identified: the atoms are distributed in a fully random distribution within a perfectly crystalline NP displaying (111) facets.
As the temperature increases, gold‐ and copper‐enriched zones appear at the surface of the NP.
Between 1000 and 1200 K, the proportion of copper and gold at the surface becomes predominant and the complete transition from solid to liquid state is observed.
Around ≈1000 K the concentration of nickel and cobalt atoms drops drastically (below 0.1%), while that of platinum is close to zero.
The surface energy, which is directly linked to this difference in energy between surface and bulk atoms, can be considered a major driving force behind segregation.
Coalescence occurs, after a few ps, with the formation of a NP whose surface is again highly enriched in copper and gold atoms.
The gold concentration at the surface is presented in both situations, showing a more pronounced segregation in the structure after coalescence.
A higher D self is revealed in the neck region close to the interface between the two NPs.

evidence_spans: Molecular Dynamic (MD) simulations are performed using the open source Large‐scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulators (LAMMPS) package.
In order to investigate Cu‐Au‐Co‐Ni‐Pt NPs, the Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potential derived by Zhou et al. is used to describe the interaction between different atomic pairs.
To validate this approach, we carried out comparisons with another EAM‐type potential, i.e., Foiles et al.
We choose to consider an equiatomic system and not the concentration observed experimentally, in order to be close to the high entropy alloy definition.

Furthermore, we perform MD simulations based on the Verlet algorithm with a timestep of 1 fs combined with the Nose‐Hover thermostat at a given temperature (including a temperature damping parameter equal to 100 timesteps) for the integration of equations of motion in the NVT canonical ensemble.
Prior to dynamic simulations, the NPs were relaxed at 0.01K using a conjugated gradient method until convergence of the total energy to get the equilibrium configuration.

Regarding the MD simulations at a given temperature, the evolution of both the total energy and the surface concentration of each element is monitored and considered complete when these two quantities reach a plateau.

Finally, all the quantities analyzed (surface concentration, atomic energy, diffusion, etc.) are derived from the averages of a set of configurations (corresponding to approximately the last 50 ns of simulations) where the plateau is reached.
Knowing that thermodynamic equilibrium is difficult to achieve at low temperature, complementary simulations were reproduced at lower heating rate (1K ns −1 ).
Furthermore, different initial configurations were considered to ensure that the initial preparation did not affect our results.
As seen experimentally, HENA prepared by PLD are FCC multi‐twinned nanostructures and many NPs present an icosahedral shape.
we investigate NPs in an icosahedral structure having a five‐fold symmetry and containing 309, 923, 2057, and 3871 randomly distributed on the FCC multi‐twinned lattice.
This corresponds to cluster sizes ≈2 to 5 nm close to the range explored experimentally.
This last point is illustrated in Figure S17 (Supporting Information) where the gold segregation in case of an icosahedron and truncated octahedron of the same size is presented.
